title: WHY THE NUMBER 1 ALWAYS POINTS BACK TO GOD ALONE
paragraphs: WHY THE NUMBER 1 ALWAYS POINTS BACK TO GOD ALONE
Before there was a second thing to compare Him with, God was. And when everything you have built your life around finally disappears, He will still be God.
There is something strangely uncomfortable about the number one.
Not because the number itself possesses mystical power. It does not.

The Bible never tells Christians to hunt for secret messages in license plates, clocks, receipts, dates, repeating digits, or “angel numbers.” Biblical faith is not numerology. We do not need 1:11 on a clock to know God is speaking when He has already given us His Word.
But Scripture does repeatedly confront us with a truth expressed through the language of one.
One God.
One Lord.
One faith.
One body.
One hope.
One Mediator.
One name through whom salvation comes.
And once you understand what Scripture is actually saying, “one” stops being merely something you count.
It becomes a confrontation with everything competing for the throne of your heart.
Because the biblical message is not that the numeral 1 has supernatural power.
The message is infinitely greater:
God has no rival.
Before your career existed, God was.
Before anyone knew your name, God was.
Before your first heartbreak, God was.
Before your greatest failure, God was.
Before the secret you are terrified somebody will discover, God was.
Before the universe had a sunrise, an ocean, a human heartbeat, or a single voice capable of whispering His name…
God was.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Because most of us would never say, “I worship another god.”
We know better than that.
We know the vocabulary.
We know the songs.
We know when to say “Amen.”
We know how to share the verse.
We know how to look faithful in photographs.
But an idol does not need a temple anymore.
Sometimes it has your password.
Sometimes it appears in your bank balance.
Sometimes it is the relationship you cannot surrender.
Sometimes it is the opinion of people whose approval controls your emotions.
Sometimes it is success.
Sometimes it is ministry.
Sometimes it is your reputation.
Sometimes the idol staring back at you from the throne is…
you.
That is why one of the most important declarations in all Scripture begins with a command to listen.
שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
Shema Yisrael, YHWH Eloheinu, YHWH echad.

“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.”
—Deuteronomy 6:4
The Hebrew word אֶחָד — ’eḥad (echad) means “one.” In its context, this confession calls Israel away from the gods of the nations and toward exclusive covenant loyalty to YHWH.
Notice the first word.
Shema.
Hear.
Listen.
Pay attention.
This is not trivia for theologians.
This is truth demanding a human response.

Israel lived surrounded by nations filled with gods. Gods for fertility. Gods for storms. Gods for harvest. Gods for war. Gods carved from wood and stone and carried into temples by the very human beings who supposedly depended upon them.
Then into that world came this thunderous confession:
YHWH echad.
The LORD is one.
You do not need another god for another part of your life.
You do not need God for Sunday and something else for Monday.
You do not need God for eternity but money for identity.
You do not need Jesus for forgiveness but human applause for worth.
You do not need Christ for heaven while keeping control as lord of earth.
He is not one option sitting among your other loyalties.
He is God.
And Jesus did not abandon this confession.
When asked about the greatest commandment, Christ began by repeating Israel's confession that the Lord is one, and then called us to love God with the totality of our being.
Not with the religious portion.
Not with whatever remains after ambition has taken its share.
Not with the leftovers after entertainment, relationships, money, ego, lust, resentment, and anxiety have eaten first.
All.
Heart.
Soul.
Mind.
Strength.
That word “one” eventually becomes frightening because it forces a question few of us want to answer:
If God is truly God alone, why does He receive so little of me?
Read that again without rushing.
Why does the One who gave you breath sometimes receive only the moments when you cannot breathe?
Why does the One who gave you life sometimes hear from you only when your life is falling apart?
Why does the One who gave His Son receive whatever time remains after you have given hours to things you will not remember ten years from now?
Why are we capable of scrolling until 2:00 a.m. but suddenly exhausted after six minutes of prayer?
Why can someone's rejection ruin an entire week while Christ's acceptance barely changes our afternoon?
Why can a number in a bank account determine whether we feel secure when Jesus told us our Father knows what we need?
Perhaps our greatest idols are not the things we kneel before.
Perhaps they are the things we cannot imagine living without.
And now the knife reaches deeper.
Because you can remove an idol from your hands while secretly keeping it in your heart.
You can delete the number and still worship the memory.
You can leave the relationship and still live for their approval.
You can give away the money and still crave status.
You can preach Christ and secretly worship being recognized as someone who preaches Christ.
You can serve God while becoming addicted to people noticing that you serve God.
You can build a ministry supposedly for Jesus and slowly begin needing the ministry more than Jesus.
That is how subtle idolatry becomes.
It does not always say, “Reject God.”
Sometimes it whispers:
“God can stay. Just don't let Him be first.”
But biblical Christianity will not permit Jesus to become a decorative addition to a life still ruled by self.
Paul writes:
ἀλλ’ ἡμῖν εἷς θεὸς ὁ πατήρ
all’ hēmin heis theos ho patēr
“For us there is one God, the Father…”
and then:
καὶ εἷς κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός
kai heis kyrios Iēsous Christos
“…and one Lord, Jesus Christ.”
—1 Corinthians 8:6
The Greek word εἷς — heis means “one.”

Paul writes those words in a discussion about idols. His point is not mystical arithmetic. He is drawing a dividing line between the many supposed “gods” and “lords” of the surrounding culture and the Christian confession of the one God and the one Lord, Jesus Christ. Paul says that all things are from the Father and that all things are through Jesus Christ.
That changes everything.
Jesus is not your motivational accessory.
Jesus is not merely someone who helps you become a more successful version of yourself.
Jesus did not endure the cross so that you could sprinkle Christianity over a life whose true center remains you.
He is Lord.
And suddenly the scandal of grace appears.
Because if God alone deserves the throne, every one of us has committed treason.
Every time I chose my sin over His command.
Every time I knew what Scripture said and deliberately walked the other direction.
Every time I wanted His blessings without His authority.
Every time I wanted forgiveness without repentance.
Every time I wanted heaven without holiness.
Every time I wanted Jesus as Savior while resisting Jesus as Lord.
I was not merely “making mistakes.”
I was taking what belonged to God and placing something else there.
Sometimes myself.
And perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
Maybe nobody knows what happened last night.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your parents do not know.
Maybe your church does not know.
Maybe the people who admire your faith would be stunned if they could see your private history.
Maybe you have learned how to lift your hands while hiding chains.
Maybe you have become exceptionally good at appearing spiritually alive while something inside you is starving.
And somewhere beneath all that Christian language is the fear you almost never admit:
If people really knew me, would they still love me?
There is an even more important question.
Does Jesus know?
Yes.
Every chapter.
Every deleted message.
Every compromise.
Every hidden appetite.
Every night you promised God it would be the last time.
Every prayer you prayed and then violated.
Every mask.
Every wound.
Every ugly thought you wish you could erase.
He knows.
And He went to the cross knowing.
That is the scandal.
The holy God you displaced from the center came looking for rebels.
The King we dishonored came wearing flesh.
The Lord we resisted walked toward a cross.
Jesus did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was so devastating that reconciliation required a price we could never pay.
At Calvary, grace does not pretend your rebellion was beautiful.
Grace exposes how terrible sin really is…
and then shows you how much greater Christ is.
This is where “one” becomes breathtaking again.
Scripture says:
“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
—1 Timothy 2:5
One Mediator.
Not your goodness.
Not your religious résumé.
Not your pastor.
Not your church attendance.
Not your generosity.
Not your suffering.
Not your morality.
Not your family name.
Not your ability to promise that you will “do better next time.”
Jesus Christ.
The sinner does not climb his way toward God.
God came down.
The guilty do not negotiate their acquittal.
Christ bears the judgment.
The dead do not resuscitate themselves.
Christ gives life.
The lost do not become their own road home.
Jesus says He is the way.
That is why the Gospel is simultaneously offensive and magnificent.
It destroys our pride before it heals our shame.
It tells the moral person, “You cannot save yourself.”
It tells the broken person, “Your sin does not have to be the final chapter.”
It tells the proud, “Bow.”
It tells the ashamed, “Come.”
It tells the sinner, “Repent.”
It tells the forgiven, “Rise.”
It tells the wounded, “Your scars do not get to name you.”
And it tells every human heart:
There is one throne. Stop trying to sit on it.
Maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
Because you are tired.
Tired of controlling everything.
Tired of maintaining the image.
Tired of pretending the addiction is manageable.
Tired of telling everybody “I'm okay.”
Tired of trying to be your own savior.
Tired of carrying tomorrow before tomorrow arrives.
Tired of fighting battles in your imagination that God never commanded you to fight.
There is only one God.
And perhaps one of the greatest freedoms you will ever experience is finally admitting:
I am not Him.
You do not have to control the universe tonight.
You do not have to know how every chapter ends.
You do not have to force every person to understand you.
You do not have to make everyone stay.
You do not have to manufacture your own redemption.
You need Christ.
Jesus prayed to the Father:
“And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.”
—John 17:3, KJV
Notice what eternal life is described as.
Knowing God.
Not merely knowing about God.
You can know Bible stories and not surrender.
You can memorize verses and remain proud.
You can understand theology and still secretly cherish sin.
You can know church culture without knowing the Shepherd's voice.
Christianity is not fundamentally an information transfer.
It is reconciliation with God through Christ that transforms the human being.
And that transformation has consequences.
If God is one, your life cannot remain divided forever.
You cannot continually say, “Jesus owns this room, but He cannot enter that one.”
My worship belongs to You, Lord…
but not my relationship.
My Sunday belongs to You…
but not my sexuality.
My songs belong to You…
but not my money.
My public life belongs to You…
but not my private browser history.
My future belongs to You…
as long as You choose the future I already wanted.
Eventually Christ reaches the locked door.
And He does not expose it because He delights in humiliating you.
He exposes what is killing you because He loves you too much to call bondage freedom.
Repentance is not God saying, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps I will love you.”
Repentance is the sinner turning from sin toward the God whose mercy is offered in Christ.
Grace is not permission to keep your idols.
Grace brings you home to the One your idols could never replace.
So what sits in the center of your life right now?
Do not answer quickly.
What are you most afraid to lose?
Whose opinion controls you?
What do you run toward when you are empty?
What do you protect even when obedience requires surrender?
What makes you say, “God can have everything except that”?
There it is.
Perhaps that is the door.
And Christ is standing on the other side of your excuses.
Not calling you toward destruction.
Calling you home.
This is why our theme at Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same impossible beauty:
Because Scripture is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted believers.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Again and again, human scandal collided with divine mercy.
Grace did not rewrite their past by pretending it never happened.
Grace rewrote what their past was allowed to become.
And Jesus still does that.
Your worst chapter does not intimidate the Author.
Your shame does not shock the Savior.
Your sin must be confessed, not romanticized. Your rebellion must be repented of, not renamed. But when a sinner comes to Christ in faith, the answer is not self-redemption.
The answer is Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years trying to turn yourself into somebody worthy of being loved by God.
Stop negotiating with grace.
Come empty-handed.
One God.
One Lord.
One Mediator.
One Savior.
And one sinner reading these words who may finally be tired enough to stop running.
Maybe that sinner is you.
Sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not. Christ alone saves.
Send this to the believer who is exhausted from pretending.
There is only one God—and you were never required to become Him.

If you genuinely want to glorify God, let that desire become more than a slogan. Glorifying God includes faithful stewardship, generosity, encouragement, sharing truth, serving others, and supporting sound Gospel work as the Lord enables you.
And there is something else worth knowing.
Bring your family.
Bring the friend asking difficult questions.
Bring the Christian who has gone cold.
Bring the person who does not believe yet.
Bring the person quietly wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them after everything they have done.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting God Himself.
God does not need our money to remain God.
God was God before Gospel Warrior existed.
God will remain God when every platform disappears.
We give because He first gave.
We serve because Christ served.
We share because someone shared the Gospel with us.
We support Gospel work because the Gospel is worth carrying.
And we worship because there is only One worthy of the throne.
So tonight, before you close this article, imagine your heart as a room.
One throne stands in the center.
Look carefully at who—or what—is sitting there.
Your career?
Your fear?
Your relationship?
Your reputation?
Your wounds?
Your money?
Your lust?
Your need to be admired?
Your need to control everything?
Your own reflection?
Now look beyond the throne.
There is a cross.
And on that cross is the One who did what none of your idols could ever do.
Money could not bleed for you.
Approval could not forgive you.
Pleasure could not reconcile you to God.
Success could not carry your guilt.
Control could not conquer death.
Your reputation could not rise from the grave.
Jesus did.
And the risen Christ does not merely offer to become another important part of your crowded life.
He calls you to Himself.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Let the idols fall.
Let the masks fall.
Let the excuses fall.
There is one God.
There is one Lord.
And there is grace for the sinner who finally stops running.
Follow because your soul needs truth more often than your feed gives it.
remember the One Name we are trying to point toward.
Jesus Christ.
Because someday the applause will stop.
The numbers will disappear.
The possessions will change hands.
The body will return to dust.
The kingdoms we spent our lives building will belong to someone else.
And all the little gods we were terrified to surrender will finally reveal how powerless they always were.
But God will still be God.
Christ will still be Lord.
Grace will still have been grace.
And the question will never have been whether you managed to become important enough.
The question is whether you belonged to the One who is.
When everything you thought you needed finally becomes nothing, may you discover that the One you surrendered everything to was always enough.
